cells.tense: Right now, what you want and what feels fair are pointing the same way.
cells.verb: weighing what's right and what's owed, quietly, from the inside
cells.place: in the direction you've been steering toward
cells.ask: gather one thing that's already ripe on this road — let what you've outgrown end, and count what it left you.
cells.core:
Right now, what you want and what feels fair are pointing the same way. You're not talking yourself into the direction and you're not talking yourself out of it — the pull toward it sits right in your gut, and your gut is the one doing the checking. That agreement is rare and it's real.
It also means something has been growing while you steered. There's a thing on this road that's ripe, and taking it would mean letting an older version end. If you want it: gather that one thing, honor what it closes, and see what the ending leaves in your hands.
cells.sheetLine: Wanting it and knowing it's right have stopped arguing.

cells.tense: You're already deciding you won't have earned it.
cells.verb: weighing what's right and what's owed, over and over
cells.place: in the direction you want to go
cells.ask: let one person hold a piece of the weighing — hand them one question about this direction and take their steadiness as an answer. What comes back is a sense of what's right that doesn't need the arithmetic.
cells.core:
You're already deciding you won't have earned it. The thing you're drawn toward is clear enough, but before you can take a step you run it through the ledger — who it's fair to, what it costs, whether wanting it is allowed — and the ledger never closes. The checking has gotten ahead of the walking.
Fairness you keep recomputing stops being fairness and becomes a toll. If you want a way through: let one person hold a piece of this with you. Give them one question about the direction and lean on their steadiness rather than your own count. What tends to come back is the plain sense of right you had before the math started.
cells.sheetLine: You're auditing whether you deserve it instead of going.

cells.tense: The inner check on direction has gone quiet, and you're still standing where it stopped.
cells.verb: weighing what's right and what's owed
cells.place: in the pull toward what you want
cells.ask: show one person a plain way through something you know, this week — give direction instead of waiting for it. What comes back is your own sense of right, speaking up again without being pushed.
cells.core:
The inner check on direction has gone quiet, and you're still standing where it stopped. You still feel pulled toward things, but the part of you that says this one's fair, that one isn't, isn't weighing in — so you follow whichever pull is loudest and feel odd about it after. The wanting is still running. The weighing isn't.
Forcing yourself to feel it again won't start it. What tends to work is the sideways route: pick one thing you understand clearly and lay out a plain path through it for someone else, step by step, this week. Giving direction wakes the part of you that knows direction. The compass comes back on its own schedule, and when it does, right and wrong are simple again.
cells.sheetLine: Plenty of pull, and the inner check on it has gone quiet.

cells.tense: You're already steering by what sits right with you — you just call it something else.
cells.verb: weighing what's right and what's owed, without saying so
cells.ask: name one direction you took and say what you knew before you justified it — then let that knowing stand without the argument. What comes back is a sense of right you can simply trust.
cells.core:
You're already steering by what sits right with you — you just call it something else. The turns you take toward some things and away from others aren't luck and aren't just taste; a private sense of fair is doing the choosing. You explain them afterward as circumstance, and the explaining is doing more work than the knowing ever needed.
If you want to see it: pick one direction you took and say, plainly, what you knew before you built the reason. Then don't defend it. Knowing that's yours doesn't need a case; it just proves out. When you own that, fairness stops being a thing you reason toward and goes back to being a thing you feel.
cells.sheetLine: You've been steering by what's fair and calling it circumstance.
